screens.title: Load Balancing with ProxySQL
screens.subtitle: Use an intelligent MySQL proxy to route, pool, and optimize database traffic

narration.text: In this chapter we explore ProxySQL, an open-source, high-performance proxy that sits between your application and MySQL servers. You will understand why teams add ProxySQL to their stack: it parses S Q L, applies routing rules, pools connections, and can offload reads from the primary. We will walk through the architecture, how to configure users and hostgroups, and how to write query rules for read/write splitting. You will also see how ProxySQL can integrate with Group Replication or an InnoDB Cluster so routing adapts when primaries change. Practical configuration examples will show the exact S Q L inserts used in ProxySQL's administration interface, and we will cover monitoring the stats tables that reveal connection pools and query digests. Finally, we’ll highlight common mistakes to avoid — for example, rule order problems or firewall issues blocking the client port. By the end of this lesson you will be able to plan a ProxySQL deployment, create basic read/write rules, and verify traffic routing in a test environment. Consider how this proxy adds a layer of control and a safety net for scaling MySQL reads.

keyIdea.title: What you will learn
keyIdea.text: ProxySQL inspects and routes SQL, supports connection pooling and read/write splitting, and integrates with MySQL high-availability topologies to improve performance and resilience.

narration.text: In this chapter you will gain four practical skills that prepare you to add ProxySQL to a MySQL architecture. First, you will be able to explain ProxySQL's architecture and the benefits it brings, such as query inspection, routing, and connection pooling. Understanding these core pieces helps you decide when a proxy is appropriate. Second, you will learn to install and configure ProxySQL to accept client connections and define mysql_users and mysql_servers; this includes loading configuration to runtime and persisting it to disk. Third, you will implement read/write splitting: you will write query rules that identify read statements and send them to replica hostgroups while directing writes to the primary hostgroup. Fourth, you will learn to monitor ProxySQL using its admin interface and stats tables, and to troubleshoot common configuration mistakes like incorrect regex rules or network firewall issues. Each objective focuses on hands-on commands, verification queries, and practical checks so you can test safely in a staging environment. These competencies ensure you can deploy ProxySQL thoughtfully and verify that traffic flows as intended.

screens.title: What is ProxySQL and why use it?
screens.subtitle: A concise definition, capabilities, and typical use cases

narration.text: ProxySQL is an open-source, high-performance database proxy for MySQL that sits between applications and backend MySQL servers. At its core it inspects S Q L, enforces routing rules, and maintains connection pools to reduce backend overhead. That means you can offload read traffic to replicas, cache or rewrite queries, and centralize access control through proxy users. A practical example is a web application with heavy read traffic: adding ProxySQL lets you route SELECT statements to read replicas, freeing the primary to handle writes. Another benefit is connection pooling — instead of thousands of short connections to MySQL, ProxySQL keeps pools open to backends which reduces latency and server C P U load. A common misconception is that ProxySQL replaces MySQL native HA features; it does not. Instead, ProxySQL complements replication and Group Replication by adding intelligent routing and observability. When planning a deployment, consider network placement so application servers connect reliably to ProxySQL, and be mindful of transaction boundaries — some multi-statement transactions that mix reads and writes should be sent to the primary to preserve consistency. In short, ProxySQL is an operational control plane for query routing and pooling, useful whenever you need granular routing policies and improved connection efficiency.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: ProxySQL inspects SQL and routes queries, provides connection pooling, and centralizes routing logic to improve scaling and resilience.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › What is ProxySQL
Definition and capabilities
  • Parses SQL and applies user-defined query rules to route or rewrite queries.
  • Maintains connection pools to backend MySQL servers to lower connection overhead.
  • Groups backend servers into hostgroups for logical routing of reads and writes.
  • Provides an admin interface for runtime inspection and persistent configuration.
Analogy
Think of ProxySQL as a traffic controller that inspects each SQL request and sends it to the correct lane.
Concrete example
A high-traffic API uses ProxySQL to route SELECTs to replicas. The primary handles INSERT and UPDATE. As read queries increase, Replica CPU is utilized instead of overloading the primary.
Key Takeaway

ProxySQL is a control layer for routing and pooling, not a replacement for MySQL clustering features.

Common mistake
Assuming rule order is irrelevant. Specific rules like matching SELECT must be evaluated before general patterns.

screens.title: ProxySQL components and runtime model
screens.subtitle: mysql_users, mysql_servers, query rules, hostgroups, and admin interface

narration.text: ProxySQL exposes a set of configuration tables that define its runtime behavior. The most important are mysql_users, which defines credentials applications use to authenticate to the proxy; mysql_servers, which lists backend MySQL instances and assigns them to hostgroups; and mysql_query_rules, which inspect S Q L and decide destination hostgroups, rewrites, or caching. ProxySQL also has an admin interface, typically on port 6032, where you connect to read and write these tables. After inserting or modifying rows, two common operations are required: load the changed table into runtime so the proxy begins using it immediately, and save the configuration to disk to persist it across restarts. Connection pooling and monitoring are visible through runtime statistics like stats_mysql_connection_pool and stats_mysql_query_digest. A typical architecture places ProxySQL in the application tier network so all app connections go through the proxy listening port, then the proxy maintains pooled connections to each backend. Remember that ProxySQL evaluates query rules in order, so careful numbering or insertion order ensures specific patterns are matched before catch-all rules. This component model gives deterministic control over routing while leaving MySQL alone to handle storage and replication.

keyIdea.title: Runtime model
keyIdea.text: ProxySQL uses config tables for users, servers, hostgroups, and rules, and requires load-to-runtime and save-to-disk steps to apply changes safely.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › ProxySQL Components
Key tables
  • mysql_users — application credentials and default hostgroup.
  • mysql_servers — backend host entries with hostgroup_id and weight.
  • mysql_query_rules — pattern matching, destination hostgroup, and apply flag.
  • Admin interface — runtime inspection on port 6032 and client port typically 6033.
Load to runtime and save to disk are separate steps: make changes, LOAD ... TO RUNTIME; then SAVE ... TO DISK.
Architecture visual (cards)
Application
Connects to ProxySQL client port.
ProxySQL
Holds config tables, pools connections, evaluates rules.
Primary hostgroup
Receives writes.
Replica hostgroup
Receives routed reads.
Key Takeaway

ProxySQL’s tables are the source of truth for routing; always validate changes with runtime stats before saving.

screens.title: Connection pooling and performance gains
screens.subtitle: How ProxySQL reduces connection overhead and improves throughput

narration.text: Connection pooling is a major operational benefit provided by ProxySQL. Instead of each application request opening a fresh TCP and MySQL handshake to a backend server, ProxySQL maintains a pool of open connections to each backend. When the application sends a new client connection, ProxySQL reuses an existing backend connection from the pool. This reduces C P U and latency cost on MySQL servers and decreases socket churn. A simple mental model: pool connections are worker threads waiting for work, while client connections are short-lived sessions that attach and detach. The ProxySQL admin runtime exposes stats_mysql_connection_pool so you can monitor active and free connections per host. A concrete example: a burst of 1,000 short queries from many clients can overwhelm the backend with connection setup cost; with ProxySQL pooling, backend servers see a steady number of persistent connections instead. However, pool sizing matters — setting too few pooled connections can create a bottleneck, and too many can exhaust resources. A common misconception is that pooling hides latency entirely; it reduces connection setup costs but does not eliminate query execution time. Always monitor pool metrics and backpressure behavior during load tests before moving rules into production.

keyIdea.title: Pooling benefits
keyIdea.text: ProxySQL pools backend connections to reduce handshake overhead and improve throughput, but pool sizing must be validated under load.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Connection Pooling
How pooling works
  1. ProxySQL maintains persistent connections to backends.
  2. Client sessions are mapped onto these persistent backend connections.
  3. When a client finishes, the backend connection returns to the free pool.
Pro Tip
Watch stats_mysql_connection_pool to tune min and max connections per host to match workload.
Concrete scenario
A REST API with many short-lived requests reduces load on MySQL by using ProxySQL pools. Instead of 10,000 new backend connections per minute, ProxySQL reuses 200 persistent connections.
Key Takeaway

Pooling reduces connection overhead, but test pool size to avoid becoming the bottleneck.

screens.title: Read/Write splitting with mysql_query_rules
screens.subtitle: Pattern matching, rule order, and directing traffic to hostgroups

narration.text: Read/write splitting is implemented in ProxySQL using mysql_query_rules. Each rule includes a match pattern, destination hostgroup, and an apply flag. ProxySQL inspects S Q L and evaluates rules in order to determine routing. A canonical setup is to create a rule that matches SELECT statements and sends them to a replica hostgroup, followed by a catch-all rule that routes everything else, typically writes, to the primary hostgroup. For example, a rule matching the start of a statement can use a caret anchor that matches SELECT at the beginning. Remember that order matters: specific rules must be evaluated before generic patterns. A common mistake is inserting the catch-all first, which would prevent the more specific SELECT rule from ever matching. Be careful with complex queries or comments — pattern matching should be tested with representative queries from your application. Transactions that mix reads and writes may require routing to the primary to avoid stale reads; you can write rules to detect transaction state or simply route certain session types to the primary. Always test rule behavior in staging and verify the effective destination using stats or connection logs.

keyIdea.title: Rule ordering
keyIdea.text: Write specific match rules (e.g., SELECT) before general rules; the mysql_query_rules evaluation order determines routing.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Read/Write Splitting
Rule anatomy
  • match_pattern — regex to match SQL text.
  • destination_hostgroup — where matching queries are sent.
  • apply — whether the rule applies when matched.
  • rule_id / order — evaluation sequence matters.
Common mistake
Placing a general '.*' rule before a more specific '^SELECT' rule will swallow matches and misroute queries.
Example and verification
-- Rule: SELECT => hostgroup 20
INSERT INTO mysql_query_rules (rule_id, active, match_pattern, destination_hostgroup, apply) VALUES (1, 1, '^SELECT', 20, 1);
-- Catch-all: everything else => hostgroup 10
INSERT INTO mysql_query_rules (rule_id, active, match_pattern, destination_hostgroup, apply) VALUES (2, 1, '.*', 10, 1);
LOAD MYSQL QUERY RULES TO RUNTIME; SAVE MYSQL QUERY RULES TO DISK;
Key Takeaway

Order your rules so that the most specific patterns run first, and always verify rule effects in staging.

screens.title: Configuring users and backend servers
screens.subtitle: mysql_users and mysql_servers — exact commands and considerations

narration.text: Configuring ProxySQL requires adding application users and defining backend servers. In the admin interface you insert rows into mysql_users to create credentials that applications use against ProxySQL. Each mysql_user can specify a default_hostgroup so queries with no matching rule have a destination. Backend servers are added via mysql_servers with a hostgroup_id, hostname, port, and weight. After making inserts, two operations are essential: load the altered table into runtime, which activates the new configuration immediately, and save the table to disk to persist across restarts. A typical pattern is to use hostgroup 10 for primary writes and hostgroup 20 for read replicas. In practice, confirm that the same application user exists on the backend MySQL instances with matching passwords and permissions. If backend credentials are incorrect, ProxySQL will be unable to establish pooled connections. A concrete example shows inserting one primary and two secondaries, then loading mysql_servers to runtime and saving. Always test by connecting a MySQL client to ProxySQL and running a SELECT and an INSERT to observe routing. This hands-on configuration step is the basis for any read/write splitting strategy.

keyIdea.title: Config commands
keyIdea.text: Insert mysql_users and mysql_servers rows, then LOAD to runtime and SAVE to disk; ensure backend credentials match and permissions are correct.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Configuring Users & Servers
Add application user
INSERT INTO mysql_users (username, password, default_hostgroup) VALUES ('app_user', 'app_password', 10);
LOAD MYSQL USERS TO RUNTIME; SAVE MYSQL USERS TO DISK;
Note: Ensure the same user exists on backend MySQL instances.
Add backend servers
-- Primary (writes)
INSERT INTO mysql_servers (hostgroup_id, hostname, port, weight) VALUES (10, '192.168.1.10', 3306, 100);
-- Replica (reads)
INSERT INTO mysql_servers (hostgroup_id, hostname, port, weight) VALUES (20, '192.168.1.11', 3306, 100);
LOAD MYSQL SERVERS TO RUNTIME; SAVE MYSQL SERVERS TO DISK;
Key Takeaway

Always verify backend connectivity and credentials after adding servers to avoid connection failures.

screens.title: ProxySQL vs MySQL Router
screens.subtitle: When to choose ProxySQL over MySQL Router and common distinctions

narration.text: ProxySQL and MySQL Router both sit between clients and MySQL, but they target different operational needs. MySQL Router is simple and closely tied to InnoDB Cluster, providing straightforward routing and integration with the cluster mechanism. ProxySQL, in contrast, is a general-purpose proxy offering query inspection, rewrite, caching, and sophisticated query rules. Choose ProxySQL when you need granular control over which queries go to which hostgroups, connection pooling, or when your topology includes replication, Group Replication, or sharded environments. A misconception is thinking one is strictly better than the other; it's about fit. If you run a pure InnoDB Cluster deployment and prefer minimal configuration, MySQL Router may be preferable. If you need rule-based routing, read/write splitting, and connection pooling across diverse topologies, ProxySQL is the better match. In practice, teams sometimes use both: Router for cluster-aware routing and ProxySQL for advanced traffic shaping. The important decision is aligning features with operational needs and the complexity you are prepared to manage. ProxySQL vs MySQL Router means use proxysql when you need advanced query routing, pooling, and rules; use mysql router for simple innodb cluster integration.. In practical terms, when to choose proxysql over mysql router and common distinctions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choose by need
keyIdea.text: Use ProxySQL when you need advanced query routing, pooling, and rules; use MySQL Router for simple InnoDB Cluster integration.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › ProxySQL vs Router
ProxySQL
  • Query inspection and rewrite capabilities.
  • Connection pooling and caching options.
  • Flexible hostgroups for complex topologies.
MySQL Router
  • Lightweight proxy focused on InnoDB Cluster integration.
  • Simpler configuration and topology awareness.
  • Less fine-grained query routing.
Practical rule
Pick the tool that matches your requirements: advanced routing and pooling → ProxySQL; minimal cluster-aware routing → MySQL Router.

screens.title: Integrating with Group Replication and InnoDB Cluster
screens.subtitle: How ProxySQL complements MySQL high-availability topologies

narration.text: ProxySQL can be configured to understand Group Replication or InnoDB Cluster roles and adapt hostgroup assignments as primaries change. Using the mysql_group_replication_hostgroups table or dynamic monitoring, ProxySQL can map group members to hostgroups automatically so that the primary receives writes while secondaries receive reads. This is useful because group membership may change during failover, and ProxySQL's dynamic updates reduce manual reconfiguration. A concrete setup uses hostgroup IDs designated for primary and secondary roles; ProxySQL's monitoring detects a new primary and updates the hostgroup mapping. One important caveat: in multi-primary Group Replication configurations, care is needed when defining read/write strategies because write consistency semantics differ. Another practical point is to test failover scenarios in staging so you can observe how ProxySQL updates its runtime servers and how application traffic is routed during role changes. In summary, ProxySQL adds an adaptive routing layer on top of the cluster, giving operational teams flexible control while the cluster handles data consistency and replication. Integrating with Group Replication and InnoDB Cluster means proxysql can dynamically track group membership and map primaries and secondaries to hostgroups to handle failover and topology changes.. In practical terms, how proxysql complements mysql high-availability topologies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Integration benefit
keyIdea.text: ProxySQL can dynamically track group membership and map primaries and secondaries to hostgroups to handle failover and topology changes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › MGR & InnoDB Cluster
Dynamic hostgroup mapping
ProxySQL can use group replication metadata to assign primaries to write hostgroups and replicas to read hostgroups, enabling automated routing when roles change.
Test failover behavior: confirm ProxySQL updates runtime_mysql_servers and that client traffic follows the new primary.
Practical caution
Multi-primary setups change consistency expectations. Decide whether certain transactions should always go to a designated primary to avoid conflicts.
Why it matters
Combining ProxySQL with MGR provides resilience and routing flexibility without replacing the cluster’s replication behavior.

screens.title: Monitoring ProxySQL runtime and stats
screens.subtitle: Which tables to query to verify connections, routing, and query digests

narration.text: Monitoring ProxySQL is done through its admin interface and a set of runtime and stats tables. Key tables include stats_mysql_connection_pool, which shows pooled connections per backend; stats_mysql_query_digest, which provides top queries and their routing behavior; and runtime_mysql_servers, which shows currently active backend servers. To validate configuration, query these tables after executing representative client traffic. For example, after running a SELECT, you should see activity in stats_mysql_query_digest indicating that the query was matched and routed to the replica hostgroup. If an INSERT does not reach the primary, check runtime_mysql_servers to confirm the primary's entry and verify backend credentials. Another important check is to ensure the client listening port, typically 6033, is reachable from application hosts; a firewall blocking this port is a common external cause of connection failures. Use the admin interface to examine connection pool sizes and adjust settings based on observed free vs. used connections. Always test changes in a staging environment and use these stats to reason about whether rules and pool sizes match your workload. Monitoring ProxySQL runtime and stats means use stats_mysql_connection_pool, stats_mysql_query_digest, and runtime_mysql_servers to validate routing, pooling, and server health.. In practical terms, which tables to query to verify connections, routing, and query digests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Monitoring tables
keyIdea.text: Use stats_mysql_connection_pool, stats_mysql_query_digest, and runtime_mysql_servers to validate routing, pooling, and server health.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Monitoring & Stats
Query digest example
SELECT * FROM stats_mysql_query_digest ORDER BY cnt DESC LIMIT 10;
SELECT * FROM stats_mysql_connection_pool WHERE hostgroup=20;
These queries show top queries and connection pool usage per hostgroup.
Verification checklist
  • Confirm SELECTs appear in stats_mysql_query_digest routed to replica hostgroup.
  • Confirm INSERTs go to primary hostgroup in runtime_mysql_servers.
  • Check stats_mysql_connection_pool for free vs used connections.
Key Takeaway
Use runtime stats to verify that query rules behave as expected and that pools do not become a bottleneck.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting steps
screens.subtitle: Regex pitfalls, firewall issues, credentials, and transaction boundaries

narration.text: Troubleshooting ProxySQL often comes down to a few recurrent issues. First, regex patterns in mysql_query_rules can be too broad or misordered; if a general pattern is evaluated first it will prevent specific matches. Always test rules with representative queries. Second, backend credentials or missing users can prevent ProxySQL from opening pooled connections. After adding mysql_users and mysql_servers, verify backends accept the configured user. Third, network factors are common: if applications cannot reach ProxySQL’s client port, they will see connection failures even though backend servers are healthy. Check firewalls and network ACLs. Fourth, transaction boundaries require caution: complex transactions mixing reads and writes might get inconsistent results if reads are routed to replicas. In such cases, route the entire transaction to the primary. A useful troubleshooting sequence is: check runtime_mysql_servers for active servers, query stats_mysql_connection_pool for pool health, review stats_mysql_query_digest for rule matches, and finally test application queries to observe actual routing. This stepwise approach helps isolate whether a problem is rules, credentials, network, or application-level behavior. Common mistakes and troubleshooting steps means verify rule order and patterns, backend credentials, network access to client port, and transaction routing to avoid stale-read issues.. In practical terms, regex pitfalls, firewall issues, credentials, and transaction boundaries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting checklist
keyIdea.text: Verify rule order and patterns, backend credentials, network access to client port, and transaction routing to avoid stale-read issues.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Troubleshooting
Top causes
  • Incorrect regex order in mysql_query_rules.
  • Backend credential mismatch preventing pooled connections.
  • Firewall blocking ProxySQL client port.
  • Mixing reads and writes in transactions without routing to primary.
Step-by-step debug
  1. Check runtime_mysql_servers for expected backends.
  2. Inspect stats_mysql_connection_pool for pool anomalies.
  3. Query stats_mysql_query_digest to see which rules matched.
  4. Test app-level queries to reproduce the issue and verify routing.
Common mistake
Assuming backend health implies client connectivity — always check the client-facing port and firewall rules first when facing connection failures.

screens.title: Hands-on: Configure basic read/write splitting
screens.subtitle: A guided checklist and starter commands for a staging lab

narration.text: This hands-on activity guides you through setting up basic read/write splitting in a staging environment. Begin by installing ProxySQL on a Linux VM and connecting to the admin interface using the admin user. Next, add an application user into mysql_users and set default_hostgroup to the primary hostgroup. Then insert backend servers: add your primary to hostgroup 10 and one or more replicas to hostgroup 20. After adding users and servers, load each table to runtime and save it to disk. Create two mysql_query_rules: a specific rule that matches SELECT statements and sends them to hostgroup 20, and a catch-all rule that routes the rest to hostgroup 10. Remember rule order: the SELECT rule must be evaluated first. Test by connecting a MySQL client to ProxySQL’s client port and running a SELECT and an INSERT; check stats_mysql_query_digest and stats_mysql_connection_pool to confirm the routing. Finally, simulate a failover in staging and observe how ProxySQL updates server lists; adjust monitoring queries so you can detect role changes in production. This stepwise activity helps you validate both configuration and operational behavior. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Compact definitions you should keep handy

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to remember about ProxySQL. First, ProxySQL is a high-performance proxy that inspects S Q L and applies routing rules, which you use to control where queries go. Second, a hostgroup is a logical grouping of backend servers; you assign backends to hostgroups like primary and replicas so rules have clear destinations. Third, mysql_query_rules are the configuration mechanism for matching queries and routing them — rule order and pattern specificity determine behavior. Keep these three concepts front and center when designing a ProxySQL deployment. They form the basis of read/write splitting, monitoring, and integration with high-availability topologies. When in doubt, validate rule behavior in a staging environment using the admin stats tables before applying changes to production. These concise definitions will guide your practical work and troubleshooting in real deployments.

keyIdea.title: Essential concepts
keyIdea.text: ProxySQL routes queries using hostgroups and query rules; rule order is critical to correct routing.

screens.title: Key Commands and Tables
screens.subtitle: Short reminders of the commands and runtime tables you will use

narration.text: Keep a short reference of the most-used commands and tables handy when working with ProxySQL. The admin interface is typically accessed on port 6032 to INSERT into mysql_users, mysql_servers, and mysql_query_rules. After changes, LOAD the table to runtime and then SAVE to disk. For monitoring, stats_mysql_connection_pool shows pool usage, stats_mysql_query_digest summarizes top queries and matches, and runtime_mysql_servers lists the currently active backend servers. When testing read/write splitting, run representative SELECT and INSERT queries and inspect these tables to confirm routing. Treat this page as a checklist you can use during a lab or when validating behavior in staging before applying changes to production. Key Commands and Tables means use insert + load + save for config; query stats_mysql_connection_pool, stats_mysql_query_digest, and runtime_mysql_servers for verification.. In practical terms, short reminders of the commands and runtime tables you will use. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Key Commands & Tables
Config Commands
INSERT INTO mysql_users/mysql_servers/mysql_query_rules; then LOAD ... TO RUNTIME; SAVE ... TO DISK;
Monitoring Tables
stats_mysql_connection_pool, stats_mysql_query_digest, runtime_mysql_servers
Ports
Admin interface default 6032, client listening default 6033 — ensure firewall rules permit access.
Final Tip
Validate rule effects with runtime stats and test failover scenarios in staging to ensure reliable behavior.

ai_generation_note: Create a 12-minute live coding video. Start with a brief architectural diagram of ProxySQL between an app and a primary/secondary MySQL setup. Then, demonstrate installing ProxySQL on a Linux VM. Walk through connecting to the admin interface and adding `mysql_users`, `mysql_servers` (primary and two secondaries in different hostgroups), and `mysql_query_rules` for read/write splitting. Show testing the setup by connecting a MySQL client to ProxySQL and running `SELECT` and `INSERT` queries, verifying routing using ProxySQL's `stats_mysql_connection_pool` and `stats_mysql_mysql_query_rules` tables. Use split-screen for terminal and MySQL client. Highlight the importance of rule order. End with a reflection prompt: "How would you adapt these rules for a multi-primary Group Replication setup?"
